| Measure | Duty on foreign molasses | How it was enforced |
| Molasses Act, 1733 | 6 pence per gallon | Rarely collected; smuggling was widespread |
| Sugar Act, 1764 | 3 pence per gallon | Strictly enforced; violators tried in admiralty courts without juries |

books.section: B. Debt and Taxation Following the French and Indian War
The Sugar Act, the Currency Act, and the Stamp Act

stem: Why did a law that lowered a tax still anger colonists?

options.text: It moved smuggling trials from local juries to admiralty courts without juries
It doubled the price of sugar and rum in colonial markets
options.misconception: The duty was cut in half, so prices did not double — the anger was about enforcement and courts, not about the price of sugar.

options.text: It forbade all colonial trade with the French West Indies
options.misconception: Trade with the French West Indies continued — the act taxed it and enforced the tax, it did not forbid it.

options.text: It required colonists to pay the duty in gold rather than in paper money
options.misconception: The Sugar Act said nothing about gold — the Currency Act of 1764, a separate law, restricted colonial paper money.

rationales.A: Background: the anger was about the courts, not the rate. Admiralty courts tried smugglers before a single judge with no jury — and to colonists, trial by jury was a right of Englishmen that Parliament was taking away.
rationales.B: The rate fell, so the price did not double. The anger came from enforcement, not from the cost of sugar.
rationales.C: The French West Indies trade was taxed, not forbidden. The molasses still arrived; now the Crown collected on it.
rationales.D: Gold was never part of the Sugar Act. The paper-money restriction came from the separate Currency Act of 1764.
rationales.general:
1. Start with the surprise. A lower tax angered people — so the rate cannot be the reason.
2. Look at the enforcement column. Violators were tried in admiralty courts — Background: before a single judge, with no jury.
3. Ask what the colonists lost. Not money, but a right: trial by a jury of their peers, which they counted among the rights of Englishmen.
Remember: people rarely revolt over a price — they revolt when a procedure tells them their rights no longer count.
